title: Scoring the pilot of That Was the Week That Was
summary: Jones arranged the pilot, which was a smash, and describes how the humor changed from Kennedy to Johnson.

blocks.x: This is February 8th, 1978, and we're going to go through your resume here, Jimmy, and pick up the things that we sort of may have skipped over. One of them was that I understand you arranged the music for the pilot show of 'That Was the Week that Was.'
Yes. Yes, I did the whole show, and it
was a smash. But I didn't get the regular assignment. Someone else got it. Well, you know the political things that happen.
Uh-huh.
So I just kept marching on. I didn't pay any attention, you know.
You mentioned when we were talking about it a few minutes ago that when you started working on it John F. Kennedy was alive, and during the time you were working on it, is that right --
Well, John F. Kennedy was in -- he was in the White House at the time.
Uh-huh.
And by him having a great sense of humor it gave the script writers more latitude, you know.
Uh-huh.

And they could write funnier things, personal things, you know. But after he was killed and President Johnson came in, and they had to change the style, because there was a different personality in the White House. And it wasn't just about the White House itself, but it was just about current events in general.
Uh-huh.
And we had one fellow, I never did know his name. He had to write some French music. And on profile he looked just like De Gaulle. Yeah, you know, and that was
about De Gaulle, you know?
Uh-huh.
And then there was -- I forget what Henry Fonda and Henry Morgan said on there. Then we had Nichols and May, Elaine May and -- you know, the film director.
Uh-huh. Mike Nichols.
Yeah. They were an act then, you know?
Yeah. They came out of the Second City, Compass Theater in Chicago.
Let's see. As I keep talking some of these names will come -- but it was a pretty heavy show.
But you said that when the Johnson Administration came in the material became more careful?
Yes.
A bit Less liberal, because Johnson didn't have the kind of sense of humor that Kennedy had.
No. So you have to adjust to these things in show business, you know.
Uh-huh.
As you adjust to different audiences in different places.
